title: A.F.A. Tours, Inc. v. Whitchurch (1991)
summary: The court prematurely dismissed for an inadequate jurisdictional amount without allowing the tour company to establish the value of its claimed losses and requested relief.
notes:
The dollar threshold in the historical litigation was $50,000. The course’s casebook describes the later ordinary diversity threshold separately. Keep the historical amount, the legal test, and the actual damages award distinct.

Whitchurch had worked for A.F.A. as a tour escort for about seventeen years and had escorted roughly 1,500 A.F.A. clients; the district court raised the jurisdictional amount on its own at the close of argument and granted summary judgment for Whitchurch, and the Second Circuit vacated under the rule that the sum claimed by the plaintiff controls if made in good faith unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less.

sections.Parties: A.F.A. Tours, which organized specialized tours, sued Whitchurch, a former employee who allegedly used its confidential customer information to compete.
sections.Material Facts: The business had conducted numerous tours, including trips to Australia, New Zealand, and Papua New Guinea, and had developed a customer list. Whitchurch allegedly contacted customers using information obtained through the employment relationship. A.F.A. sought damages and an injunction against the continuing conduct, as well as punitive relief. The potential injury therefore included more than the profit on one completed transaction.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed for lack of the then-required $50,000 amount in controversy. The Second Circuit vacated that dismissal and required a proper opportunity to address the jurisdictional valuation. The opinion’s numerical examples illustrated possible proof rather than awarding the amounts described.
sections.Issue: Could the court conclude to a legal certainty that the amount was insufficient on the record and procedure used?
sections.Holding: No. The plaintiff needed a fair opportunity to establish the value of the controversy, including legally relevant future losses and injunctive relief.
sections.Reasoning: The amount claimed in good faith is not defeated merely because eventual recovery is uncertain or likely to be smaller. A finding that the threshold cannot be met requires the legal-certainty standard. Where an injunction would protect continuing business interests, the value at stake cannot be reduced without analysis to the damages already realized. The district court also needed to consider whether the claimed forms of relief were legally available. The appellate court identified potential calculations to show why dismissal on the undeveloped record was premature; it did not determine that those losses had actually occurred.

learning.why: The court prematurely dismissed for an inadequate jurisdictional amount without allowing the tour company to establish the value of its claimed losses and requested relief.

topics.cp-amount-in-controversy: A court could not find the amount deficient to a legal certainty without giving the plaintiff a fair opportunity to establish the value at stake. The value of prospective relief and threatened future injury could matter to the jurisdictional amount.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: A jurisdictional valuation is distinct from the amount ultimately awarded.
topics.cp-diversity: The amount-in-controversy dispute arose in a diversity action and the legal-certainty test is the diversity threshold rule.
topics.cp-usc-1332: The case applies the section 1332 amount-in-controversy requirement (then $50,000).

mnemonic.rationale: A tour escort and the jurisdictional amount
